title: Antidepressants: Select for the Patient, Monitor Benefit, Activation, Withdrawal, and Safety
bottomLine: Antidepressant prescribing requires a correct target diagnosis, bipolar/suicide assessment, patient-specific drug selection and measurement of both response and harm. Monitor early activation/adverse effects, adequate dose/duration, adherence and discontinuation risk; do not switch or augment randomly.
recognize: Different agents vary in activation/sedation, sexual effects, weight, BP, anticholinergic/QT, interaction and discontinuation burden.
differentiate: Nonresponse may reflect wrong diagnosis, bipolarity, inadequate trial, nonadherence, substance use or untreated medical illness.
Discontinuation symptoms differ from relapse and are more likely with abrupt cessation/short half-life agents.
assessment: Review diagnosis, mania/hypomania, suicide risk, prior response, pregnancy, anxiety/pain/sleep symptoms, interactions, organ function, bleeding/hyponatremia/QT risk and patient priorities.
workup: Use targeted sodium/ECG/labs when risk/agent requires them; routine broad laboratory or pharmacogenomic testing is not required for every patient.
management: Start a guideline-supported option, optimize deliberately and switch/augment according to CANMAT response/tolerability sequencing.
Psychotherapy and combined treatment remain important according to severity and preference.
medicationSafety: Monitor emerging mania, serotonin toxicity, suicidality/activation, hyponatremia, bleeding/BP/QT and withdrawal according to agent/patient.
Consider overdose toxicity and quantity when acute suicide risk is relevant.
counselling: Explain time to benefit, common early effects and why abrupt stopping can cause symptoms.
followUp: Measure symptoms/function/adverse effects after initiation/titration and document rationale for switch/augmentation.
examTrap: Adding a second antidepressant after a brief low-dose trial without checking adherence, bipolarity or adequate duration.
oneLinePearl: Antidepressants need a diagnosis, an adequate trial and a measurement plan—not serial guesswork.

title: Antipsychotics: Target the Syndrome, Monitor Metabolic and Neurologic Harm
bottomLine: Antipsychotic treatment requires a defined psychotic/mood target and planned metabolic, movement, cardiovascular and agent-specific monitoring. Choose the lowest effective burden that supports recovery; do not use antipsychotics routinely for insomnia, uncomplicated anxiety or dementia behaviours without narrow justification.
recognize: Weight/metabolic changes, akathisia/parkinsonism/tardive dyskinesia, prolactin effects, sedation/orthostasis and QT risk vary among agents.
differentiate: Akathisia can mimic anxiety/agitation; NMS is a medical emergency rather than worsening psychosis.
Delirium/dementia agitation requires cause/environment assessment before reflex antipsychotic use.
assessment: Confirm target diagnosis/symptoms, prior response/EPS, weight/BMI/waist, BP, glucose/A1C/lipids, cardiac/QT risks, prolactin symptoms, smoking/substances, pregnancy and interactions.
workup: Use metabolic measurements and movement-disorder assessment longitudinally; ECG/prolactin/other tests are agent/risk specific.
Clozapine uses current Canadian hematologic/clinical monitoring pathways rather than obsolete U.S. REMS assumptions.
management: Use shared-decision evidence-based antipsychotic therapy with psychosocial rehabilitation; optimize one agent before unnecessary polypharmacy and use clozapine when treatment-resistant schizophrenia criteria/monitoring allow.
medicationSafety: Monitor NMS, severe EPS/tardive dyskinesia, metabolic disease, QT/orthostasis and clozapine neutropenia/myocarditis/seizure/constipation risks.
counselling: Explain expected benefit, metabolic/movement monitoring and why abrupt discontinuation can destabilize illness.
followUp: Track symptoms/function, movement/metabolic measures and ongoing indication; simplify polypharmacy when possible.
examTrap: Treating new restlessness as worsening psychosis and increasing the antipsychotic without considering akathisia.
oneLinePearl: Antipsychotic monitoring follows the whole patient—not just hallucinations.

title: Mood Stabilizers: Lithium, Valproate, Carbamazepine, and Lamotrigine Need Different Monitoring
bottomLine: There is no generic 'mood stabilizer monitoring.' Match efficacy and toxicity surveillance to the actual agent, mood polarity, organ function, pregnancy potential and interactions. Lithium levels never override clinical toxicity; valproate reproductive risk and lamotrigine severe-rash risk must be actively managed.
recognize: Lithium is effective for bipolar maintenance/mania and has a narrow therapeutic index; valproate/carbamazepine/lamotrigine have distinct episode roles and toxicities.
differentiate: Lamotrigine is useful for bipolar depression/maintenance but not acute mania; lithium toxicity can occur with levels previously tolerated when renal/sodium/fluid status changes.
assessment: Review mood polarity, pregnancy potential, renal/hepatic/thyroid status, sodium/fluid changes, interacting drugs, prior rash and adherence.
workup: Lithium uses serum level plus renal/thyroid/calcium and clinical monitoring; valproate uses hepatic/CBC/reproductive context; carbamazepine uses CBC/liver/sodium/interactions; lamotrigine is titration/rash focused.
management: Choose/titrate according to bipolar episode/maintenance evidence and patient risk; reinforce hydration/sick-day/interactions for lithium and slow lamotrigine titration.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, diuretics and dehydration can raise lithium toxicity risk.
Valproate has major teratogenic/reproductive risk; serious lamotrigine rash/mucosal symptoms require urgent evaluation.
counselling: Teach agent-specific toxicity signs, interaction/sick-day rules and contraception/pregnancy planning.
followUp: Monitor mood plus agent-specific labs/levels and reassess as renal function/medications/pregnancy status change.
examTrap: Calling a lithium level 'therapeutic' and dismissing tremor, ataxia and vomiting after dehydration/NSAID exposure.
oneLinePearl: Mood stabilizers share a goal, not a monitoring plan.

title: Benzodiazepines: Narrow Indications, Short Exposure, Interaction and Withdrawal Safety
bottomLine: Benzodiazepines can be useful for selected acute indications but are poor default long-term treatment for anxiety or insomnia. Before prescribing, assess substance use, respiratory/falls/cognitive risk and concurrent opioids/alcohol; if dependence is established, taper gradually rather than abruptly stopping and precipitating withdrawal/seizures.
recognize: Sedation, psychomotor impairment, falls, memory problems, tolerance and physical dependence increase with exposure/risk factors.
differentiate: Physical dependence is expected with repeated use and is not identical to benzodiazepine use disorder.
Alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal can be medically dangerous unlike uncomplicated anxiety rebound.
assessment: Confirm indication, duration/prior use, opioid/alcohol/other sedatives, OSA/COPD, falls/cognition, pregnancy, driving/work risk and substance-use history.
workup: No routine labs diagnose dependence; use targeted toxicology/organ testing when clinical context requires it.
management: Prefer evidence-based psychotherapy/maintenance alternatives for chronic anxiety/insomnia.
For chronic use without ongoing benefit, use collaborative gradual taper individualized to dose/duration/withdrawal history.
medicationSafety: Opioids/alcohol and benzodiazepines markedly increase respiratory/overdose risk; abrupt withdrawal can cause severe anxiety, autonomic symptoms and seizures.
counselling: Discuss driving/impairment, dependence and tapering honestly without stigmatizing prescribed use.
followUp: Reassess ongoing indication and taper progress; monitor withdrawal and function rather than automatic refills.
examTrap: Abruptly stopping long-term high-dose benzodiazepines because the medication is high risk.
oneLinePearl: High-risk prescribing is not fixed by high-risk withdrawal—taper safely.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Geriatrics/Hospital Pharmacy recommendations

title: Mental Health in Primary Care: Safety, Longitudinal Diagnosis, Treatment, and Integration
bottomLine: Primary care can diagnose and longitudinally manage many common mental-health conditions when safety, diagnostic uncertainty, comorbidity and treatment response are actively reassessed. Every visit should preserve the ability to detect suicide risk, bipolarity, psychosis, substance use and medical contributors rather than reducing care to medication refills.
recognize: Depression/anxiety/insomnia/substance use frequently present through somatic or functional concerns.
Continuity allows diagnostic evolution and measurement-based treatment adjustment.
differentiate: Primary-care management is appropriate for many stable conditions; severe mania/psychosis, imminent suicide risk, complex eating disorders or treatment-resistant illness may require specialty/acute care.
assessment: Assess symptoms/function, safety, bipolarity/psychosis, substances, sleep/trauma, medical/medication contributors, supports and treatment preference.
workup: Use validated scales as adjuncts and targeted labs only for plausible medical mimics; avoid broad psychiatric testing panels.
management: Use evidence-based psychotherapy/medications, collaborative goal setting and regular follow-up; integrate chronic disease, reproductive and substance-use care.
medicationSafety: Reconcile psychotropics at every transition and monitor class-specific metabolic, organ, interaction and withdrawal risks.
redFlags: Failure of multiple adequate treatments with diagnostic uncertainty
counselling: Normalize mental health as longitudinal medical care and involve supports with consent.
followUp: Track function/symptoms and ensure specialty referrals/pending assessments are closed-loop.
examTrap: Continuing serial antidepressant refills for years without ever reassessing diagnosis, bipolarity, substance use or functional outcome.
oneLinePearl: Primary mental-health care is longitudinal clinical reasoning—not prescription maintenance.

title: Collaborative Mental Health Care: Shared Plan, Measurement, Communication, and Escalation
bottomLine: Collaborative care works when primary care, mental-health specialists and allied professionals share a treatment plan, measurement, communication and escalation rules. A referral without feedback/ownership is not collaborative care.
recognize: Psychotherapy access, medication management, social needs and medical comorbidity often require multiple disciplines.
differentiate: Co-location alone does not create integrated care; collaboration requires defined roles and closed-loop information flow.
assessment: Identify diagnosis/severity, safety, functional goals, barriers, current team, patient-preferred supports and who owns medication/therapy/follow-up.
workup: Use shared symptom/function measures when useful to track response across the team; tests remain diagnosis driven.
management: Create one care plan with clear roles, communication interval, treatment targets and escalation threshold; use psychiatric consultation for complexity while maintaining primary-care continuity when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Avoid duplicate/conflicting psychotropic prescribing across teams; reconcile after ED/hospital/specialty changes.
redFlags: Rapid deterioration awaiting routine specialty appointment
counselling: Explain team roles to the patient and preserve consent/privacy boundaries for information sharing.
followUp: Track whether referrals occurred and recommendations were implemented, not merely whether they were sent.
examTrap: Assuming a patient is safe because a psychiatry referral was placed despite no appointment, no safety plan and no interim follow-up.
oneLinePearl: Collaborative care needs shared ownership, not shared paperwork.

title: Mental Health Crisis Intervention: Safety, De-Escalation, Medical Causes, and the Least Restrictive Effective Plan
bottomLine: In a mental-health crisis, stabilize medical threats, assess suicide/violence/psychosis/intoxication and capacity, use calm trauma-informed de-escalation and choose the least restrictive setting that can actually maintain safety. Medication/restraint is not a substitute for assessment or environmental de-escalation.
recognize: Agitation can result from psychosis/mania, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, trauma, pain, hypoxia/hypoglycemia or interpersonal crisis.
differentiate: Delirium/medical instability changes the pathway from purely psychiatric management.
Distress without imminent danger may be safely managed outpatient only when supports/follow-up are real.
assessment: ABCs/vitals/glucose/medical screen when indicated, suicide/violence/means, psychosis/mania, substances/withdrawal, capacity, dependents, supports and triggers.
workup: Use targeted tox/metabolic/injury/infection testing according to presentation; do not delay immediate safety/stabilization for exhaustive testing.
management: Use verbal/environmental de-escalation, remove weapons/means, involve supports/security/EMS as appropriate and use emergency psychiatric care when safety cannot be maintained.
Use medication/restraint only when clinically justified, monitored and consistent with law/policy.
medicationSafety: Sedation choice requires respiratory/cardiac/substance context and ongoing monitoring; avoid stacking sedatives without reassessing response.
counselling: After stabilization, explain the plan, preserve dignity and include the patient's priorities where possible.
followUp: Every discharge from crisis requires a concrete safety/medication/follow-up plan with ownership.
examTrap: Escalating sedative medication for an agitated hypoglycemic/delirious patient before identifying the medical cause.
oneLinePearl: Crisis care is safety plus diagnosis plus de-escalation—not sedation alone.

title: Mental Health Referral: Escalate for Risk, Diagnostic Complexity, Treatment Resistance, or Specialty Therapy Need
bottomLine: Referral is driven by risk and complexity, not diagnostic label alone. Emergency referral is required when safety or medical stability cannot be maintained; specialty referral is appropriate for diagnostic uncertainty, severe/complex illness, treatment resistance, specialty medications/therapies or major functional deterioration. Referral never transfers responsibility before care is actually received.
recognize: Psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe eating disorders, recurrent self-harm, complex substance use and treatment-resistant mood/anxiety often need specialty input.
differentiate: Routine consult differs from emergency psychiatric assessment; waiting months is unsafe for active suicide/mania/psychosis or rapid deterioration.
assessment: Define risk, diagnosis/uncertainty, treatments tried with dose/duration/adherence, comorbidities, function, supports, substances and urgency.
workup: Complete appropriate basic medical/substance evaluation before referral when safe, but do not delay emergency transfer for diagnostic perfection.
management: Use emergency services for imminent danger/medical instability; use psychiatry/addiction/eating-disorder/trauma/perinatal/early-psychosis specialty services according to need.
Maintain interim treatment/safety follow-up until handoff is closed.
medicationSafety: Do not initiate specialty/high-risk medication outside competence/monitoring capacity merely because the referral wait is long; coordinate bridging treatment safely.
counselling: Explain why referral is recommended and what the patient should do if symptoms worsen before the appointment.
followUp: Confirm appointment/consult outcome and integrate recommendations; retain ownership of unresolved safety issues.
examTrap: Assuming responsibility ended when a referral was faxed despite ongoing high suicide risk and no appointment.
oneLinePearl: A referral is not a handoff until someone accepts the clinical work.
sourceBasis: Canadian mental-health referral and collaborative-care practice
